items.title: A Path Forward on AI Safety for the United States and China
items.summary: AI safety in parallel means creating touchpoints and information channels between the United States and China that strengthen the safety capabilities of each side. In practical terms, this could mean limited and strategic sharing of emerging threats and the best practices for detecting and mitigating dangerous AI capabilities. These exchanges can happen through the upcoming U.S.-China governmental dialogue and, for less sensitive areas of engagement, nongovernmental Track II dialogues between [...] Compared with some of the more ambitious proposals for international governance—a non-proliferation treaty for AI, for example—AI safety in parallel is modest in its goals. It treats binding agreements between the countries as a bonus rather than the immediate goal. Depending on where the technology goes in the coming years, this might well prove insufficient. If that’s the case, we will need to adapt quickly. But we have to start somewhere, and beginning with the mental model of safety in [...] Both the U.S. and China have experience worth sharing on AI safety and governance. Technical research on frontier AI safety has deep roots here in the United States but is a relatively newer field in China. One of the most valuable things that could come out of U.S.-China engagement on AI would be sharing approaches to testing for dangerous new capabilities in models: the ability to discover novel pathogens or to intentionally evade the control of a human operator.

items.title: Industry Leaders Unite in Open Secure AI Alliance for AI Safety and Security
items.summary:
As policymakers and regulators grapple with AI safety, it will be crucial to recognize open models, harnesses and security tooling as defensive assets, not liabilities, in AI and cybersecurity policy. Blanket restrictions on open frontier AI systems would weaken defensive capacity and risk concentrating power, dependence and vulnerability in a few closed providers. [...] Real AI safety and security depend on the full agent stack — identity, permissions, harnesses, guardrails, logs and evaluation — not just on whether model weights are open or closed. Open harnesses and tools make those controls easier for many defenders to inspect, test and improve.

NVIDIA is contributing open models, model weights, data and new agent harness research to the Open Secure AI Alliance to speed the development of new cybersecurity tools and techniques. [...] The age of AI agents can be one of resilience and shared security. With the right choices, open secure AI systems can give defenders the tools they need, strengthen competition, extend technological leadership and ensure that the safety and security of this extraordinary technology are built in the open for everyone.

items.summary:

If we want to create a safety framework that will truly prioritize getting in place a national and international standard—which is what will best support the safe deployment of AI—it will take hard work, a seriousness of purpose and a strategy that connects the states, the federal government, and the international conversation. A performative or virtue signaling approach will not get the job done [...] Second, companies developing the most capable systems should meet clear requirements, including independent audits, incident reporting, strong security standards, and whistleblower protections.

Third, federal and state efforts should reinforce one another. State laws will not all be identical, and we look forward to working with policymakers across the country to ensure they strengthen safety while maximizing AI’s economic benefits. [...] OpenAI’s frontier safety blueprint lays out what we believe are the essential elements of that framework.

First, the federal government should lead the testing and evaluation of the most advanced systems. Frontier AI raises national security and public safety questions that require technical expertise, resources, and access that no state can fully replicate.

items.title: Quantum computing at scale could be here soon - PitchBook
items.summary: # Quantum computing at scale could be here soon. ## Oratomic, which just raised a $300M Series A, is building quantum computing that could lower the barrier of entry for mass use. A new era in quantum computing could be coming sooner than expected, if startup Oratomic, which just raised $300 million in Series A funding, is to be believed. Investors’ excitement over Oratomic stems from the company’s bold claim and goal: to build a fault-tolerant quantum computer faster and with fewer resources than existing methods—and to finally make quantum computing truly useful at scale. Quantum machines have long been sought after for their unique ability to handle tasks that are too complex for modern computers. This particularly applies to cracking complex encryptions with Shor’s algorithm, a method that involves factoring large numbers to break a key, which can only be done with a quantum computer. VC funding for quantum computing startups has been on a tear.

items.title: Quantum Computing Is Emerging as a Tool for Tomorrow’s Electrical Grids - POWER Magazine
items.summary: ##### Sign In. Home Technology Quantum Computing Is Emerging as a Tool for Tomorrow’s Electrical Grids. # Quantum Computing Is Emerging as a Tool for Tomorrow’s Electrical Grids. But as electrical grids become more distributed, data-intensive, and renewable-heavy, some of the most complex decision-making problems are becoming harder to manage with existing approaches alone. The case for quantum computing is not that classical methods are collapsing. That is why power systems are emerging as one of the most promising application areas for hybrid quantum-classical computing. The most promising applications are not routine grid simulations or generic data processing tasks, but complex optimization workflows where even incremental improvements in solution quality, speed, or scenario coverage could have operational and economic value. Quantum computers are not expected to replace classical computing infrastructure in grid operations. Instead, the more realistic path is hybrid computing: classical systems continue to perform the tasks they do well, while quantum algorithms are tested as accelerators or enhancement layers for specific optimization problems.

items.title: New quantum simulation breakthrough could accelerate fault-tolerant computing - Digital Journal
items.summary: A newly published study from researchers at the University of Southern California (USC) and Los Angeles–based startup Quantum Elements could mark an important step toward practical quantum computing. This is a development with implications that extend into Canada’s rapidly growing quantum ecosystem. At its core, the research addresses one of the most pressing challenges facing the quantum computing industry: how to manage and correct errors in inherently fragile systems. The problem is that the computational requirements scale exponentially with the number of qubits, quickly becoming unmanageable. The USC–Quantum Elements team has developed a new Quantum Monte Carlo (QMC) algorithm that addresses this bottleneck. The newly published method suppresses a long-standing issue known as the “sign problem,” which has historically limited the efficiency of Monte Carlo simulations in quantum systems. One of the most significant implications of the work is its application to so-called “digital twins”, which are virtual replicas of quantum hardware.

items.title: Singapore, IBM partner on defence quantum computing - Janes
items.summary: # Singapore, IBM partner on defence quantum computing. The Singapore Ministry of Defence (MINDEF) has partnered with IBM to advance quantum computing and assess its potential military applications. MINDEF announced on 21 July that its Defence Science and Technology Agency (DSTA) and the Singapore Armed Forces' (SAF's) Digital and Intelligence Service (DIS) will collaborate with IBM to evaluate the use of quantum computing for complex mission planning, including logistics optimisation. As part of the collaboration, DIS and DSTA engineers will receive cloud-based access to IBM's quantum computing resources and work alongside IBM specialists to build in-house expertise, MINDEF added. The partnership forms part of MINDEF's broader efforts to advance and integrate quantum technologies. In March 2025, MINDEF and Singapore's National Quantum Office launched the Quantum Sensing Centre (QSC) to facilitate research and development (R&D) and integration of quantum technologies for position, navigation and timing (PNT), remote sensing (RS) and biomedical sensing and imaging (BSI) applications.

items.title: Quantum Computing Stocks: D-Wave, AT&T Expand Quantum Agreement - Investor's Business Daily
items.summary: *   IBD 50 Stocks To Watch. *   How To Invest In Stocks. # Quantum Computing Stocks: D-Wave, AT&T Expand Quantum Agreement. **D-Wave Quantum** (QBTS) on Monday announced an expanded commercial agreement with telecom giant **AT&T** (T). D-Wave shares popped on the news with earnings due for quantum computing stocks in early August. Under the expanded agreement, AT&T will use D-Wave's quantum computing technology to address complex telecom network optimization challenges. "AT&T's initial focus is on layering D-Wave's annealing quantum computing technology into the tools that are already powering AT&T's agentic AI solutions," the companies said in a news release. One application of using quantum computing and agentic tools in AT&T's network are improving network operations will be in outage detection and management. "AT&T plans to explore using D-Wave's quantum computing technology across a broader set of applications, such as outage detection and response, technician routing, network build planning, and traffic management," the companies said. On the stock market today, D-Wave stock popped 7.5% to 17.43.
